text:
Common Health Problems Of Cats If you are new to owning a cat, you may be surprised to find that health problems are a common thing. No matter what breed of cat you own, health problems are to be expected. Some can be hereditary, while others can be easily avoided.

Worms Regardless of the breed of cat, worms are a very common and recurring problem. Tapeworms, roundworms and hookworms are among the most common that infect cats. Cats that have weight gain problems, flea problems, or if you find white spots in his stool, you should ask your veterinarian to test him for worms. Although they can be treated with medication, worms can prove fatal if left untreated.

Hair balls Hairballs are the most common health problem for cats. All cats groom themselves daily, normally swallowing the loose hairs that come from their coats. Occasionally, these loose hairs will gather in a ball and lodge in the digestive tract instead of passing through your cat's stool. When your cat starts coughing and hacking, it normally spits out a hairball. Although it can be rather disgusting in the end, most cats can dislodge the hairballs without any problems.

In rare cases, a hairball can pass through the intestine of a cat, creating a blockage. Blockages are very serious problems and can be life-threatening if left untreated. If your cat becomes constipated, does not eat properly, or has a very dull coat, it could have a blockage. If you notice any of these symptoms, you should immediately take him to the veterinarian. You can prevent hairballs and blockages by brushing your cat 2 or 3 times a week to remove loose hair. You can also give him food designed to control the hairballs.

Urinary tract infection Urinary tract infection is also a common health problem in cats. Urinary tract infection is more common in male cats that have not been sterilized, although females can also suffer from this problem. When a cat suddenly stops going to its litter box, this problem is normally the cause. Another symptom is when the cat's urine begins to smell very strongly. If you suspect that your cat has a urinary tract infection, you should take it to the vet. Your veterinarian can treat the problem with medication and make recommendations to help avoid this problem in the future.

Feline leukemia In the past, feline leukemia was the biggest cause of death in cats. These days however, there are vaccines available that can treat the disease. To treat the disease, your cat will need to receive the vaccine before being exposed. Even if death does not occur immediately, cats exposed to feline leukemia normally have a long lifespan. If you know that your cat has feline leukemia, you should never allow other cats around him, as the virus is very contagious.

To protect your cat, you should always make sure to take her to the vet for her regular checkups. If you keep him informed of his vaccinations, he should lead a healthy and productive life. Although some health problems can be prevented, most of them can. You can also keep your cat indoors, which will protect it from the majority of health problems. If your cat is an outdoor cat, regular visits to the veterinarian will keep it healthy. As long as you take your cat to the vet and keep it healthy, it will be your companion for years to come.

text:
First Time Adopting - Acclimation Stage Hi I have a few questions, and they may be just super specific to my situation but I just wanted to see if anyone has had a similar experience with this and had any tips, advice or insight. We know this is perfectly normal for him to be stressed but we want to make sure we're doing everything we can for him!

We have a resident cat (4, fixed male, was an abandoned stray we started feeding and kept him) who is very chill and friendly. We decided to adopt another cat because our resident cat made friends with my friends cats who stayed long term with us and he showed signs he missed companionship for a few months. We decided to adopt our new little guy (2, fixed male) and he had lived with his foster mom since he was five weeks old. I know that every situation with every cat is different so we were prepared for a slow introduction, but we were not ready for how fearful and anxious he is. Yes, again we know this is naive but I have been extremely fortunate that with all my other experiences with cats they all have been scared for a few hours and then looked for attention. We were silly not to think this would be a possibility, considering he had only ever had one home. Here is the timeline:

Pick-Up Friday (Day 0) : He was so stressed and anxious when we picked him up, we walked in while distracting our resident and put the new cat in the bathroom. My partner checked in on him and he was burrowed under the blanket in the carrier and he was panting. I had never seen a cat pant of make the noises he was making. We decided to move him to our bedroom where the AC is a lot stronger (there's a heatwave in CA, 96F during the day, house sat at around 80F, room was around 70-75). From then on he has just been in my room full time. We also contacted his foster mom right when this was happening; she let us know this is a stress response and told us to put his toys (she gave us a bag of his favs along with his burrow blankie) pet him, along with a few more things. Petting him and our presence didn't seem to help at all so we just gave him his space, he just hid in a suitcase with his blanket over it. This was night 1 of us on the air mattress in the living room lol

Saturday (Day 1) : When the store opened I ran and got a feliway plug in, calming collar and relaxing spray. I set his things up, put his collar on (this is when he moved to the bed burrow with our comforter), when put the collar on and offered him churu he started panting again. I know it was because I exposed him in his anxious state, so again I just did what I needed to do in the room and left. Also we set up the room with his bed from his old house, toys, scattered treats around, food (wet and dry), litter box and treats. He did not use or consume anything that whole first day, his foster mom said we shouldn't be worried unless it hits Sunday and he still had not ate, drank or used the litter box.

Sunday (Day 2) : We checked in on him and saw he used the litter box and ate half the wet food we left the night before and we were so hyped!! I walked into the room in the morning and accidentally walked in on him when he was roaming and he cornered himself so I just walked out. This was bittersweet because I was happy he was exploring but also felt horrible that I scared him. He spent the day burrowed while we passively hung out in the room, we would just sit on the floor and read for 15 minutes or so. We tried reading out loud to him but us being there and our voices seemed to make his heart rate go up to we would leave.

Monday (Day 3) - gabapentin: He did not eat any of his food overnight, just some of a purr pop we set out but he did use the litter box! However whenever we went into the room to check on him and his things (food, water, litter) he would shift in the burrow and had a rapid heartbeat. At this point his foster mom gave us gabapentin and told us to give him 100mg a day (she gave us 4 doses). She also told us he has always been around other cats so maybe allowing my cat near the door would bring him comfort, it honestly did not seem to so we decided to just keep focusing on getting him used to the space. They started meowing at each other from different rooms that night. His foster mom also told me that I should try to sleep in the room, I did for about 2 hours until he fell when he was exploring, it startled me so I shot up and so it also scared him, I left so he can have his space back.

Tuesday (Day 4) - gabapentin: After the first night on gabapentin he explored, ate all the food we left him and his allergy medicine we had been worried about! This honestly was SUCH a relief that he was finally getting back to routine, we kept the same vibe of just going in to do cat chores and passively hang out. Again he just stayed burrowed but he didn't seem as stressed. We could tell he had been exploring because he was finding treats we were hiding! We also got a camera delivered.

Wednesday (Day 5) : I looked at the camera footage from last night and he did so much exploring! He also ate all of his wet food, I fed him again and he ate all of it during the day as well. I'm not sure if he is actually doing better or we just feel like he is because we can see him now, but he was active most of the night, took a nap and got back to exploring! He has also had a lot of cool snacks and was picking up some of his toys! So there is progress on the home comfort front but he's still getting used to us humans which we totally understand.

I guess I just wanted to see if you guys had any suggestions on what we can do to help our little guy out! He currently has one box, a cat tree covered in a blanket, an open suitcase with a blanket, his bed with a blanket and my bed in terms of burrows because I know this is like a big thing to get them to feel safe

Also I was hoping people could share their timelines for their scared kitties to get used to your home and start approaching you

We only had 4 doses of gabapentin that we only gave at night so who knows if his progress is also just linked to that, do you guys think once he's done with his dose he'll go back to his scared state?
